thread.title: Meet the startup Traci Des Jardins, Thomas Keller are banking on to help ease restaurant staffing woes

author: Katie Burke
title: Meet the startup Traci Des Jardins, Thomas Keller are banking on to help ease restaurant staffing woes
text: – Food/Hospitality/Retail Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Jul 12, 2018, 11:04pm PDT Spice Kit CEO Will Paccio had his lightbulb moment a few years ago when he had to jump in to make sandwiches at the chain's Palo Alto outpost after a worker quit abruptly. So Paccio, along with former Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) executive Dave Lu , launched Pared — an online staffing marketplace where restaurant operators can hire workers on a freelance basis. Whether it's a grab-and-go sandwich counter or a Michelin-starred fine-dining outpost, Bay Area restaurants are in a panic over a severe worker shortage. Turnover rates for back-of-the-house staff are as high as 120 percent, according to Instawork, far higher than the national average of 70 percent. Since it was founded in 2015, Pared has attracted about 900 restaurants across the Bay Area. Its platform has roughly 3,000 workers available for hire. Heavyweight investors include acclaimed chef Thomas Keller, Yelp (NYSE: YELP) CEO Jeremy Stoppelman , YouTube CTO Steve Chen , San Francisco 49ers CEO Jed York and Square's (NYSE: SQ) Caviar executive Gokul Rajaram. Just last week, Pared landed a $10 million Series A, led by Charles River Ventures. The round gave the fast-growing startup a $35 million valuation, according to Pitchbook. "Especially in the Bay Area, it's hard to find not just staff, but good and reliable staff," Pared President and Co-Founder Lu said. "There is an exodus of cooks and kitchen labor, and with more and more restaurants opening every day, it's getting even harder to find the folks that are reliable and with the talent and skill sets restaurants need." Here's how it works: Pared does all of the vetting, sourcing and data collection to make sure the workers on its platform can fit right into a kitchen. Restaurants pay a fee for the service in addition to the worker's wages, which start at $20 an hour — considerably higher than the city's current $15 per hour minimum wage. The startup charges more for last-minute cancellation and higher-demand time periods. Pared charges between $500 and $1,000 if a restaurant wants to hire a temporary worker for its full-time staff. Its clients includes high-end restaurants like Saison, Spruce, Lazy Bear and Atelier Crenn as well as quick-service counters at Mixt, Dabba and Salt & Straw. Chef Traci Des Jardins also uses the platform at her acclaimed Hayes Valley restaurant Jardinière. Des Jardins used to pull a 15 percent profit from restaurant, but told the Business Times that now, partly because of high labor costs, she's basically breaking even. "The restaurant model is really broken. I love it and there are lots of reasons why I want to stay in business, but any other businessperson wouldn't go near it," the James Beard award-winning chef said. She added that labor accounts for 40 percent of her operating costs. "The need for a service like this is really relevant at this moment in time," Des Jardins said. She has used Pared and hired a few staff members from it. "It gives you the ability to flex your labor, and it's a model that can be a game-changer for [restaurateurs] in that you're able to better manage your business." Pared allows her to pay workers for only the time she needs. The ability to keep a stable workforce and add or reduce the number of workers depending on peak periods is what Lu said is just one half of Pared's value proposition. The other half, he said, is making the workers on the platform just as happy. "Some restaurant workers have up to three jobs, but instead of getting paid $12 at a regular one, they can make $30 an hour for a last-minute gig on Pared. It creates a marketplace where they can test and try out different kitchens, cuisines and make some extra money," Lu said. "That's our secret sauce: matching needs with skills and making sure [workers] walk into somewhere and provide value." The San Francisco-based startup recently launched in New York, and is beginning to look to Chicago, Boston, Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., for future expansions. Sure, Pared won't entirely eliminate the Bay Area's staffing headaches, but Des Jardins said that it's a starting point. "It's a struggle, and we're all just trying to figure out what works," the chef said. "You get stuck in your own paradigm and can't come up with an idea on how to solve it. That's where tech and other models can help inform us and ultimately save the restaurant business." – Food/Hospitality/Retail Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Jul 12, 2018, 11:04pm PDT Related Content
